author: By Allison Garfield
title: Madison City Council rejects resolution supporting student protesters
text: After a week of high tensions, the Madson City Council deadlocked on a resolution supporting pro-Palestinian student protesters at UW-Madison. After a week of high tensions, the council deadlocked Tuesday night on a resolution supporting pro-Palestinian student protesters at UW-Madison.  Local Government Reporter Local Government Reporter After a week of high tensions, the Madson City Council deadlocked on a resolution supporting pro-Palestinian student protesters at UW-Madison. The Madison City Council narrowly shot down a resolution supporting University of Wisconsin-Madison student protesters after a week of high tensions and negotiations on campus . After hours of testimony from the community, including UW-Madison students and faculty, the council voted 8-8 in rejecting the resolution , which urged Chancellor Jennifer Mnookin to allow encampments to continue during ongoing negotiations with student organizers. The resolution was symbolic because the council has no oversight of the university, but it nevertheless led to a heated debate among alders and the community about the ongoing conflict in Israel and Gaza. The council meeting was Tuesday, May 7, three days before the university reached a deal with protesters to remove the encampment on Friday. Ald. Juliana Bennett, who represents downtown District 2 and formerly served as the alder for the student-populated District 8, said in an interview ahead of Tuesday's meeting that “the overall goal of the resolution is to support students, and specifically student organizers and their exercise of free speech, the First Amendment and engagement with civil disobedience, which is something that we should be prioritizing and protecting. "There’s this constant divide on council that … students are city of Madison residents and that we do represent them. It's that ongoing struggle of convincing my colleagues they cannot just take a back seat on issues because they pertain to students.” At the meeting, Bennett addressed her colleagues, many of whom were hesitant to pass a resolution that gave direction to leaders outside of the city’s jurisdiction. To Bennett, any support the city can give to students “means something,” she said. “Is it not our job to have these discussions that are of deep importance to community members? Has jurisdiction ever stopped this council from making specific statements and calls to leaders?” Bennett asked. “I'm so proud of students for making this an issue because it's given students and young people and those that don't feel represented the opportunity to be at the table at local government speaking on things that impact them.” On campus, more than 40 tents still stood on Library Mall as talks between pro-Palestinian protesters and university administrators reached an impasse Wednesday. Protesters have demanded that the university disclose all of its investments, cut ties with Israeli institutions and call for an immediate and permanent ceasefire in Gaza, among other items. University administrators continue to ask students to remove the encampment, saying it violates a state administrative code that prohibits camping on university property. Over 30,000 people in Gaza have been killed during the Israeli military's assault, by most estimates. Israel's actions are a response to a Hamas terrorist attack in October that left about 1,200 Israeli civilians dead and 240 taken as hostages. Ald. Tag Evers acknowledged “the deeply troubling moment” both Madison and the country faced as protests against the war in Gaza grew on college campuses across the U.S., as well as the awkward position of the council as an intermediary. Evers offered an alternate resolution, altering some of the stronger language in the original resolution put forward by Bennett. The alternative called upon university administrators to negotiate with student organizers “in good faith,” while also recognizing the difficult position the university is in, Evers said. “I don't believe this body should vote to cast blame for what happened last week, but instead should focus on continuing negotiations,” Evers said. “I sense that I am not the only one who is reluctant to vote for (the original resolution.) I encourage you please to consider voting for this more narrowly focused and constitutionally sound resolution.” The alternate language failed to pass with nine votes in favor and seven opposed. It required 14 votes to pass. The original resolution also required 14 votes in favor for approval, and with two alders absent and Alds. Bill Tishler and Derek Field abstaining from voting, it failed to reach that benchmark when the body split evenly. Council President Yanette Figueroa Cole voted against the resolution, citing concerns that the council is “pretending that any of these resolutions will yield accountability." “These are pretty much honorary resolutions that don't have any action attached to it,” she added. “We’re not going to get any accountability if we don’t work as a city, if we don’t work together with other agencies to ensure that the people that we serve are safe.” Alds. MGR Govindarajan, Isadore Knox Jr., Amani Latimer Burris, Mike Verveer, Marsha Rummel, Nasra Wehelie, Juliana Bennett and Jael Currie all voted in support of the resolution, while Alds. Evers, Figueroa Cole, John Guequierre, Barbara Harrington-McKinney, Charles Myadze, Regina Vidaver, Nikki Conklin and John Duncan voted against it. Madison police officers, alongside counterparts from the Dane County Sheriff's Office and the Wisconsin State Patrol, took part in the removal of protesters' tents from Library Mall on May 1 as part of a request for “mutual aid” from UW-Madison Police. But the police response to the largely peaceful protest on Library Mall escalated, resulting in numerous arrests and reports of student, faculty and police injuries. Some officers carried shields and batons, while a few others were armed with long guns. A Cap Times reporter at the scene watched as police pushed toward the tents with shields, with the protesters encircling the tents drawing together and pushing back. Some people screamed and fell to the ground. Law enforcement agencies reported that four officers were injured, one of them struck in the head by a skateboard. Every so often, attendees were handcuffed on the ground and led away by officers toward Memorial Union. In the resolution Bennett originally wrote last week, she requested that Madison Police Chief Shon Barnes adjust the department’s standard operating procedures for mutual aid to prevent city officers' use to break up peaceful protests. Established under state statute , "mutual aid" means that law enforcement personnel can provide assistance upon request from another agency within their jurisdiction and those officers are then protected as employees of that agency. The first draft of Bennett's resolution said officers should not be ordered to interfere with the lawful exercise of free speech rights and must communicate with those involved to “de-escalate and ensure the safety of event participants.” While that language was removed in a redraft of the resolution ahead of Tuesday’s meeting, Bennett said that mutual aid is still something the council should further examine moving forward. “The mutual aid conversation is something I strongly believe needs to be had and the resolution sponsors agree, which is why it was in the original resolution,” Bennett said. “However, it's something that, for the purposes of passing something now and being centered on the immediate crisis, we wanted to hold off on until a later date and time.” Earlier in the week, City Attorney Michael Haas said in a memo to the council that alders lack the legal authority to order the police department to respond to protests in a certain way. summary: The Madison City Council deadlocked on a symbolic resolution supporting pro-Palestinian student protesters at UW-Madison, a measure sponsored by Ald. Juliana Bennett that sparked intense debate.
